utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, good afternoon everybody. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. Defence teams are all present in full force. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls, Mr. Thayer. I just wanted to address you before the witness comes in. We have been informed by the Victims and Witnesses Unit that there is a possibility that the witness might feel distressed at some point in time, in which case, although he has expressed his view that he should be alone in the courtroom, they have in turn asked us possibly to allow them to be present in case he needs assistance, if he gets distressed. So I -- we have discussed that, and we will proceed first with the witness alone, but if he needs assistance, of course we'll make that available. We also had to deal with the tendering of documents of the last witness. And we agreed to postpone that until today because of some afterthought that you needed to give to the matter. Let's start with you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have three exhibits, Your Honours, as indicated on the sheet, which has been passed out. P02448, the pseudonym sheet under seal; P02452, a photograph which should remain under seal; and PIC 00070, which was the photograph marked during the testimony, and that can be -- that does not need to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? We hear none. So they are so admitted. Nikolic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. In terms of documents, there are five documents I'd like to tender into evidence. The first two documents are -- would be admitted for impeachment purposes and that would be document 3D87. 3D87 is a redacted version of the document which was previously 3D80. Now, I did not have time to give a copy to my colleague of this 3D87, and I will do that immediately at the first break. The second document is document 3D88, which is also a redacted version of the document which was used during the cross-examination called 3D81. It is also a redacted version that I will give to my colleague at the break. The next document is a document which was a Prosecution document of which we would like to tender only two pages. The number of the document is P295, P295, and we would like to tender into evidence from this document pages 109 and 110, and the pages are the same, both in English and in B/C/S. The fourth document, and this just to -- for the record, is the vehicle work log for July of 1995, concerning Victor Tango 5288 Volkswagen van. The fourth [sic] document is the log of troop presence for the brigade command, Zvornik Brigade, that's also a Prosecution document P311, and that is for the month of July 1995. The English ERN being 0084-6881. And the B/C/S ERN being 0074-3953. The fifth [sic] document we'd like to tender is the death certificate of Ruzica Pantic. This is a document that was put on the electronic court system by the Popovic team, and bears the number 1D217 or 1D217. It is a document dated 13 December 2006 and there are no ERN numbers for this document. So these are the five documents we would like to tender into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please don't interpret me as interfering in your responsibilities, but during the testimony of the previous witness, if I remember well, you asked him to mark -- put separate markings on the photo of the Grbavci school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In addition some are in red, some are in blue. In addition to the markings that he had put on the photograph that the Prosecution has tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. And this document was P1691 as marked by the witness on the second day of his cross-examination. And that was on the 23rd of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you are tendering that as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any objections on the part of...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask, Mr. Bourgon, the purpose of tendering redacted versions of statements is to tender only the parts that were dealt with during the course of cross-examination. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Judge. There are two purposes. The first is impeachment purposes. The first purpose being that we want to -- during the cross-examination, I covered with the witness the fact that during the first two interviews that were conducted with him, that first one being in December -- November of 2005, and the second one being in April of 2006, that there was a very limited references to Drago Nikolic, far less from whatever came out during his examination-in-chief. So that's the first purpose. The second purpose is to highlight those paragraphs in which he contradicted himself on the stand during his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. However, would you not agree that it would be more convenient for the Chamber to understand the -- understand the context, if the whole witness statement would be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour. I really believe that this is limited purpose for impeachment purposes and that there is no need for the complete statement to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, would it not be sufficient, those parts, as cited, quoted during the course of examination, so those will be appearing in the transcript already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, the idea is if the witness said in -- in the transcript, during his cross-examination, if the witness answered a question which was contrary to what he said in his statement, although this might have been mentioned during cross-examination, it is important to see the exact words that were used during cross-examination to be compared with those that were used when he gave his statement. Just to provide you with one example, and maybe -- I don't think it's necessary to go into closed session, but the fact that he mentioned that when he was given an order to report to the school in Orahovac, the order was given by someone called Pantic, who was the chief of transport, and that when he returned the vehicle, the vehicle was returned to a Mr. Pantic. Now, during cross-examination, of course, the story came out differently, but in the statement, he mentioned quite precisely that it was Pantic who gave the order, both to go and to whom he reported the vehicle back. So that is just one example where we feel it is necessary for the Trial Chamber to compare exactly the words of the statement with the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, one difficulty that I have there is that one of your points, as you just mentioned, was that there was limited reference to the activities or conduct of your client. In order to assess that, for my purposes, I would need to see the full statements. I take your point that not all of the evidence is being adduced, but your point was there is only limited reference in these two statements and for those purposes, for me, it would be better to have the entire statements in evidence in order to assess your point on that particular issue. That's just a difficulty that I would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I couldn't agree more.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is on. Especially since this would be in conformity along the lines of previous indications or decisions that we took on similar -- on similar issues. I mean, when it came to extracts of statements to the Prosecution, we had given you the indication that providing us only with that limited extract and not the context, the whole context in which it was made, could be disruptive and not informative enough for the purposes of our deliberations. What I suggest is that we can decide on the rest and give you a little bit more time to think it over and perhaps also discuss it with the -- with Mr. Nicholls and then we will decide on that particular document later on in the day today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I may respond to your concerns, Mr. President, and Judge. For us it is very important that those parts do not appear, and the reason is just that we want to show exactly, that out of the full statement, there is one or two lines, and these lines are maintained. So that's why I need to show with the Prosecution, or with my colleague, to show that only one line talks about Drago Nikolic in that statement and that shows even more in our point of view, the fact that out of those two interviews there were very limited references to Drago Nikolic. And that is very important for our purposes. Should the Trial Chamber decide otherwise, then we will simply not file the statement at all, because we believe that there are -- there is prejudicial information either to our client or other clients that was not raised during cross-examination that should not find itself before the Trial Chamber, even for impeachment purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you wish to comment on all that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honours. First, I don't have objections to 3, 4, 5, those exhibits. My concerns are the same as what I've heard from the Trial Chamber. I think the statements, at least -- especially the first statement at least needs to come in in full for the context. The Trial Chamber is not a lay jury. It's clear what purpose the statements are coming in for. There's a lot of cross-examination on these statements and I think the proper, normal or orthodox approach is either counsel relies on the record or the statement goes in as a whole. Part of the reason that I was willing to forego any redirect was that counsel said he was putting the witness statements in, which give the context. For instance, in paragraph 2 of the statement, the witness referred to the assistant of his boss, and how he knew him as his own name. So I think if these are coming in for impeachment, then the Chamber does need the whole context and the Trial Chamber can read and see which lines mention Drago Nikolic and which lines do not without redactions. Lastly, I've never seen these redactions. I don't know what's being offered. So I can't agree at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we will need to defer our decision on that particular document until later. So we have heard your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I would like to respond to the observations of my colleague, if you allow me to. First, we should not mix where I, the Defence, decides to file into evidence or to seek whether to admit it into evidence a prior inconsistent statement with the fact that my colleague decided yes or no to conduct re-examination. The two are unrelated. The second point is I will of course grant to him, and I said it right at the beginning, that he hasn't seen those redactions yet so he has to see them. The third issue, Mr. President, I believe that if the Trial Chamber -- we feel that it is the normal practice just to have those parts of the statement and not to have the full statement in evidence for impeachment purposes. Just to have the parts where anything that was covered during the cross-examination of the witness is still there on that witness statement. And we feel that this is the way, the best way for the Trial Chamber to be able to see what the witness said, compared to what he said on the same topics and only on the same topics in his prior inconsistent statement. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. We will come to that in due course during today's sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, you will have an opportunity to see the redacted version, and we will -- we will hear what you will have to say later, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can just say, unless the redactions are incredibly minimal, I see no prejudice whatsoever in this Trial Chamber having the full context of the prior statement and using that to compare to the testimony in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. The Popovic team, Defence team wishes to tender some documents as well. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to refer back to - thank you, Your Honours - to the proposal to tender as an exhibit the exhibit referred to by the Defence of the accused Nikolic; it is a part of the document 3D81. I would like to point out that I believe that tendering the entire document, first, I am opposed to that. Secondly, that could be harmful for the others in this case, the other accused, especially because those parts were not the subject of the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution or cross-examination by any of the Defence teams. And for those reasons, I would also like to add that the part that is being requested for tendering here is irrelevant for this case, and I absolutely believe that it cannot contribute in the slightest degree to what the Trial Chamber is meant to establish. So I believe that this information report, this report, should not be tendered as an exhibit because I believe that it can be detrimental for the other accused and that part was not the subject of the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution or the cross-examination by some Defence teams. On my part, I would also like to indicate that the list of our documents to cross-examine this witness has been handed over to the Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the purpose of the transcript, on line 23 of page 9, the document that you seem to be referring to, according to the transcript is 3D81. I suppose you meant 3D88. Can you check out for me, please, both the Nikolic Defence team and the Popovic defence team? Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, 3D88 is a redacted version of 3D81. And 3D87 is a redacted version of 3D80. Those are the two -- the two new versions bear the number 87 and 88, whereas they were 80 and 81 previously. At the break, I will immediately show my colleague those redactions and ask him to agree on the -- on having just those parts tendered into evidence. If we cannot agree, I will simply withdraw those documents because I feel they were -- the Trial Chamber can draw the same conclusions without the documents, and in addition, the fact that my learned friend did not choose to re-examine also reinforces the issue that we raised during cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. What I wanted to make clear is that we don't have before us either 3D80 or 3D81. What you seek to tender, Mr. Bourgon, is 3D87 and 3D88, and if I was reading Mr. Zivanovic well, he couldn't have been referring to 3D81 because you were not seeking to introduce 3D81 but you were seeking to introduce a part from 3D87, 3D88. So the transcript needs -- I need your confirmation of this, because I don't speak for either of you, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I didn't know that the document was in -- redacted in the meantime and that it had been given a different number. So what I said actually referred to document 3D88. That's the information report of the 10th of April, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then two submissions. I noticed Mr. Haynes standing before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was going to say I do have a document to tender into evidence but I'm conscious that there is a witness waiting to come in, so if you want to deal with it later, I will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, you need to address two issues: One is the submission by Mr. Zivanovic in relation to 3D88, which he is not seeking to tender himself, it is only a submission. The other is in relation to the five documents that he wishes to tender, namely from 1D211 to 1D214, and then your own document P1891. So let's take them one by one. And in the meantime, I would appreciate if Madam Usher could go to the room where the witness is waiting and explain to him that we've got some matters to deal with in relation to the previous witness. So that he doesn't get...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with the list. Do you have any objections to the tendering of any of these five documents? Were these put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Yes, I absolutely object to entering witness statements, which is what I believe these are, to -- to the -- into evidence at this stage. You can't -- I think they can -- witnesses can be called, but just to -- there is no need for that at all. The record was clear on this. You don't put in witness statements of other witnesses in this way. I've never seen it done. I don't agree to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in relation to 3D88? It was a submission rather than a request to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 3D88 is the redacted of 3D81, that's one I haven't seen, but I will discuss that with my colleague, as soon as I get a chance. That one, there might be a possibility for some agreement with what my colleague said. The first one, 3D80, which is the witness's ICTY statement, I find -- unless -- I find it almost impossible that would I agree to any redactions to that and I would offer it myself, if there is any -- any question, because there's been so much cross on that statement, that it may be helpful just to have it in whole to show where the witness was consistent, where he was inconsistent and as my client -- as Mr. Bourgon said, to compare the testimony, the words with what was quoted during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, these documents that you seek to tender, particularly the first four, why are you seeking to tender these documents, because they were not put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did submit to the witness that there are statements by certain survivors from a specific execution site, wishing to point out to him that there, in this other location, executions were being carried late into the night, and then they were transferred to the location that he spoke about. I explained that to him. I told him that. Others testified on that before this Trial Chamber, and statements were given also by witnesses that were not heard in court. And I had no reason to quote portions of the statements to him. He did not dispute them in any way, and I believe that they are relevant in order to assess his testimony because he said the executions at the location where he was began only after the place where the executions were carried out before that -- the meadow was completely full. And this is why I wanted to present these other statements to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just, Your Honour, looking at the transcript, I think -- I think my friend may have inadvertently misspoke. I don't think the witness ever said what is quoted here, that the executions in this place began only after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not get into that argument, please. Because that's -- may become a submission later on but not at the moment. In relation to the fifth document, the Zvornik hospital medical logbook, P1891, are you objecting to the Popovic Defence team's request to tender it into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. And I'm sorry my difficulty is we just got this, so I'm trying to make sure I know exactly what is coming in off the list. No, I don't object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This list we are in a position to decide upon straightaway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it put to the witness, Zvornik hospital medical logbook, in part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not put to the witness by me. It's a document on him being admitted to the hospital, but I cannot tender that, since the Prosecution has the same document on their list of documents that will be used to examine the witness that is coming now. It's not essential to have this document on the list now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want to contradict you, but I think, and my memory wouldn't fail me on this, we did see in the course of the testimony of the previous witness the hospital medical entry which I suppose --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I put it to him. It's P0251 [sic]. I was going to seek to put it into evidence with the qualification that it bears the name of protected witness 105 and it might have to be under seal or have that redacted. And that solves that problem. The transcript is wrong, it's P02451.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's deal with the totality of these documents. Our decision on the first four documents in the list provided by Mr. Zivanovic for accused Popovic is that we cannot exceed to the request to have them tendered. Reason is as follows: In -- if the person mentioned in this list has testified, then there is the testimony of that person that can be relied upon. And secondly, if the person mentioned hasn't testified, that's one more reason why it should not be admitted. We do admit P1891 as a Defence document. Madam Registrar, you need to pay attention to see whether this needs to go under seal or not because I am not in a position to confirm that. I don't know. As regards the document that Mr. Haynes is proposing to tender, that's P0251, correct me if the number is not the right one, Mr. Haynes, it is so admitted but it will be kept under seal because of the same reasons mentioned by Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other reason that Judge Kwon brings up and with which I associate myself, and I suppose you as well, and Judge Stole, is that to our knowledge these four witness statements were not put to the witness, were not put to the witness. Are there any preliminaries that you wish to raise before we bring in the next witness? The members of the public, I wish to advise that for a minute or so we will need to bring down the curtains, separating this courtroom from the rest, and then you will be able to follow the proceedings after that the witness has taken his place. Because the reason is that he is a protected witness. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The transcript reads on page 14, line 10, that the Trial Chamber admits P1891. I believe it is 1691, but I'm not sure. Can my colleague confirm this, because we on this end, I do not have a copy here of that photograph that was used and that was marked by the witness, but my understanding was it was 1691 and not 1891.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is a Zvornik hospital medical logbook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1891 is the Zvornik hospital medical logbook that I invited --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought this was that 1891 that referred to the photograph that was marked, because that is 1691.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So could you please bring the curtains down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you and welcome to this Tribunal. Very soon you are going to start giving evidence. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of a solemn declaration, which you are required to make before us; namely, that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth and nothing but the truth. Please go ahead, read it out loud, and that will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. We'll do our best to make things easy for you, and first thing I will do is to explain very briefly that upon the request of Prosecution, we have put in place three protective measures for you; the use of a pseudonym instead of your name and then facial and voice distortion. The whole idea is to hide your identity. I want to make sure first and foremost that this arrangement is to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer will go first. He will put some questions to you, and then some of the Defence teams will cross-examine you. Mr. Thayer. Incidentally, Witness, if at any time you need a short break, please, do let us know, and we will do our best. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon. I'm handing you a piece of paper. Please read it to yourself. For the record, that's been marked as P02449. Do you see your name printed on that piece of paper along with "PW-105"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll just pass that around. If you can, because there is a special microphone in front of you, try to sit as close to the microphone as possible, and when answering a question, whether it's from myself or my friends across the aisle or Their Honours, just take your time, wait until you've heard the entire question, and speak slowly, because we don't want to miss anything you have to say. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I know these events I'm going to ask you about are very difficult for you to talk about, but everyone here, my friends across the aisle, Their Honours, they all understand that and we just want you to try your best to answer the questions. And His Honour has already told you, if at any time you feel like you need a break, or if you feel like you need somebody here with you, please, just let us know and we'll do everything we can to accommodate you. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we may move into private session for just a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Have you explained to the witness what that means?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what year you were born in?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And your full name, I believe, was written down on that piece of paper I showed you a moment ago, but are you known by or do you go by any other name or nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Fahro.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you are a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you live in Srebrenica at sometime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell Their Honours who you lived with when you lived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: With my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you remember any other family members which you were living with at that time? If you don't right now, that's okay. I'll move on. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what your father's name was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Mehmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was he known by any other name or nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Yes. Meho.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we may revert into open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's revert to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about the events of a particular day that you told me for the first time about a year ago. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: First, would you please tell Their Honours how old were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: I was seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you please just, step by step, describe for Their Honours what you remember happening that day. And I may have to stop you every now and then to ask you a question, but please, just in your own words, describe as best as you can, what you remember happening that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: My father and I, Mehmed, were at our home, and father was screwing on a light bulb, I was looking out the window and a man was passing with an axe on his shoulder and he said that the Chetniks are coming. Father told me, hide behind -- beneath the bed. I hid, but they found us eventually. Later they took us out of the house, they forced us on to a green truck. They put some white cloth around our eyes. It became loose. I asked father to tighten it, but the Chetnik did not allow him. And that Chetnik later on tightened the blindfold very hard. He later took us to the forest, we had to lie down on our stomachs, and they opened fire at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Witness. I want to just stop you for a moment and ask you a couple of questions, okay? Do you remember anything at all about the people who put you on the truck? Can you describe at all what you recall them wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: They had the variegated uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had asked your father to tighten the blindfold on the truck. Was your father sitting next to you on the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall where in the truck you were sitting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: I was first on the side, if you were stepping out of the truck. And the father was all the way on the side, towards the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who else was on this truck, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there were any other people on the truck other than yourself and your father?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: There were many people. My father and I were not alone. There were some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you know whether some of those other people were soldiers or whether they were civilians or whether they were both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: I don't know that. I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When the truck stopped and you got out, do you remember whether it was day-time or night-time or somewhere in between?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: It was dark, it was night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I wanted to ask you some questions more specifically about what happened once you were taken out of the truck. Can you please describe for Their Honours as best as you can remember, exactly what happened when you were taken out of the truck? Witness, do you need a break? Do you think you might need a couple of minutes? I can tell you you are probably not the only one in the courtroom, if you do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: I don't need a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very well. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: I don't need a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember my question? Would you like me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: If you could repeat it. I didn't hear it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you please tell Their Honours, as best as you can remember, what happened when you were taken off the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: We left the truck and we lay down on the grass, and the Chetniks later shot at us, and one doctor came from Zvornik and he saved me. He took me to a jeep and drove me to the hospital and gave me an injection which made me sleep. I fell asleep and they sewed up my arm and my leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Witness, I just want to stop you again. When you were on the ground after you were taken out of the truck, do you remember any details about any other persons who were on the truck with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: After you were lying down on the ground, do you remember anything happening with respect to anyone else who may have been lying down on the ground at the same time as you? If you don't remember, I'll move on. You mentioned that there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did something happen to you during this shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: I cannot at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember any physical sensations after the shooting began?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to focus your attention on the time that you went to the hospital, okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: First of all, do you remember what hospital it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: In Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned that at some point you were given an injection that made you sleep. Before getting that injection, do you remember whether anyone at the hospital treated you in any way or did anything for you before the injection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: No, no, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember how long you stayed at the hospital? And I don't mean in terms of dates, but do you remember whether it was days, weeks or months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: I don't know correctly. I do not remember how long I stayed there in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned that somebody stitched you. Do you remember anybody doing anything --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- for you or to you before they stitched you, any of the nurses or doctors? If you don't remember, just say so and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: I don't -- don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe for Their Honours where on your body the doctors treated you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: My leg and my arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us which leg and which arm, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: I can, but I cannot correctly remember. I can stand up and maybe show.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you could just indicate physically and I will make it on the record which one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him do that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stand up and show us, yes. Thank you. That's not what -- it's getting confused now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said he needed to go outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him show us. Let him show us his own way. Please tell us where you -- which parts of your body you were treated for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This leg here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the witness indicates the upper part of his left thigh, on the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, I -- Your Honour, I think it may be necessary for him to be a little bit more specific than that. And it will -- and I can assure the Court, I have a reason for asking for more specificity at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where exactly on your thigh, on your -- on your leg?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you can just point to it, Witness, as specifically as you can, where on your leg the injury is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Here, here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness, in answering this question, points to his knee. Same -- same leg; left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Witness, can you point to where your other injury is located, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: My arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you just point to which arm it is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Indicating, for the record, the right biceps area, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. I think you can -- unless you want to show us something else, you may prefer to sit down, make yourself comfortable, and let's go ahead. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, with respect to the wound to your knee, can you describe the scar or marking, if any, that's there? Just describe what it's like for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a photo of it? That way you may spare him --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, not that's as useful, I think, as the description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then go ahead, try to do your best to answer the question that Mr. Thayer has put to you. If you've got problems we'll try to help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember describing for me previously what the scar on your knee is like, what it looks like, what it feels like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: I cannot. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Last week, Witness, I showed you some pictures in my office. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we see P02452, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I presume, pursuant to prior practices, this won't be broadcast, but I just, out of an abundance of caution, want to make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Alternatively, we go into private session, whichever you prefer. I have asked him to indicate his preference. If you want do it in open session, not broadcasting it, we are okay. If you want to go in private session, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can stay in open session, as long as it's not broadcast, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see a photograph on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I take it that's you in the middle, just for the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It can't be otherwise, can it? Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we may take the break now, I think that would be convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's have 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, earlier in your testimony there were some things that you said you couldn't remember, and you have had a break, and I just wanted to first ask you whether there is anything that came back to your memory during the break that you can share with Their Honours and, if there isn't, that's okay, but if there is anything that came back to you during the break about what happened, please let them know. I just have a couple more questions for you. Do you remember when we met in the home of some of your relatives about a year ago? There was a big guy named Bruce, there was myself. Do you remember that? Let me move on. Do you remember last week when somebody read to you what you told me at a previous meeting, at an earlier meeting when we met before? Do you remember somebody reading to you what you had told me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you remember that when that was read back to me, do you remember that person saying the following, which is what you told me before, "I recall that I was bathed at the hospital." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember being bathed at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please the Chamber, we have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. Ms. Nikolic or Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We have no questions for the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic or Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do not have any questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic or Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Likewise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes or Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't imagine there will be re-examination, but I will just ask for formality's sake. Do you have any questions? Sir, we have come to the end of your testimony, since no one else has any questions to put to you. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having been kind enough to come over and give testimony in this case. Our staff will assist you as required and help you to return home at the earliest. On behalf of everyone present here, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. Documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think everybody has the tender sheet. The only additions or corrections --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any objections by any of the Defence teams? We essentially have six documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The only additions or corrections, Mr. President, are that P02450 is not being tendered. In its place is P02452 which has already been admitted through a prior witness. P04251 also has been, I believe, admitted through the testimony of the prior witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? There are none. So these documents will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we just ask that they be placed under seal as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All of them under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Only this, out of an abundance of caution: P02451 appeared on page 14, line 14 of the transcript, as P0251, and has now appeared as P04251. So for the avoidance of doubt, it's P02451.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Haynes. All right. So that's decided. Ms. Frease, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: She's ready to go, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Vanderpuye is present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Ms. Frease, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye will be proceeding with his direct. We don't need to repeat the solemn declaration. You know that you are testifying pursuant to the one you made when you first started giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, I just want to welcome you back, and hopefully we won't be too long. But I did notice that you have some documents with you. I just want to make sure that we can identify for the record what those are. And if you don't mind, if you could just go through them and let us know what you have with you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the index to the intercepted radio communications that was on the CD that we provided to Defence counsel and to Your Honours. I have the index of names that accompanies that material also on the CD. I have the maps also that are on the CD, and the VRS code-names that are also included on the CD. In addition to that, I have photocopies of some conversations that are included in the CD that Mr. Vanderpuye, I -- or I believe had been given to -- to others today, but anyway, that we anticipate discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Just so that the Court is aware and Defence counsel is aware, we are actually in the process, as I speak, of copying those documents for the Defence counsel. They are documents that I believe Ms. Frease has highlighted in contemplation of her testimony that will be placed on the ELMO so everybody can see them, because they are part of the anticipated direct, but I also wanted Defence to have physical copies of them and they are being made and should be ready according to the latest update within about 20 minutes or so. Hopefully they will be here well in advance of her cross-examination. All right. Let me just take you back to your previous testimony for just a moment, if I could. Do you recall testifying that you received a series of notebooks from a commander in the 2nd Corps in 1998?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did that commander prepare a handwritten list or inventory of the notebooks that you, in fact, received?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe you testified previously that that list or the notebooks you received numbered 134 plus a diary or something like that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And at the time that you received these notebooks, were they numbered, that is physically, one through 134, 135?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have, please, 65 ter 1075 on the EDS, please. All right. Could we make this just a little bit bigger? All right. I think that's all right. Ms. Frease, first of all, is this the document that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And could you just tell us very briefly, since we've -- I think gone over some of this already, but could you just tell us from left to right what those particular designations are?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left-hand column, those are the numbers that the notebooks were numbered, so 1 through 134 plus the diary. The next column has -- indicates the number that was assigned to it by the 2 Corps and the date that they assigned that number. The next column indicates the format of the notebook. So here in most cases A5, a few were other sizes. And then the far right column indicates -- indicates when the notebooks were opened or begun.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. Have you had an opportunity to compare the number of the notebook against the next column, which you've indicated is a -- I believe it's a confidential number or something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, it's a strictly confidential number that the 2 Corps assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to compare that number against the number of the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did they conform to one another? In other words, did that number appear in the notebook that is indicated?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did that years ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you do that for 1 through 134?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And beyond 134, up to 191.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you have up until recently, been reviewing and working with the intercepts used in this particular case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you -- you've testified previously about the process of developing what you refer to as an authentication binder?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you attempt to continue the process of identifying material that corroborated the intercepts that are used in this particular case, beyond what was done with your authentication binder?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Other documents were -- I was made aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you give us an example of the type of material that you've come in -- you've been made aware of or that you've subsequently relied on or used?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of military documents and internal documents to the VRS at the time of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in assessing the reliability of the intercepts that are used in this particular case, did you rely exclusively on the corroborative documentary material that you -- that you looked at, or did you rely on other information?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On other information as well. The authentication binder was really designed to -- as a sample of the types of -- the type of material that we could draw from in order to independently corroborate some of the intercepts. So in that authentication binder we drew -- I -- at the time I drew from video, from VRS military documents, from documents from the -- from the RS ministry of the -- defence ministry, from UNPROFOR. The one big area that I didn't draw from were witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, before we get into the substance of some of those things, I would just like to focus your attention on the organisation of the intercept material that is used in this particular case, if I may. Now, you had indicated previously that you were continuing the organisation of the intercepts that are used in this case, and can you tell us -- could you tell us briefly what the process, or the result of that process was?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The result of the process was a three-binder set, or the intercepts that -- that were handed out on CD. It's a collection of about 220; I think it's 217 intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what was involved in the organisation of that set of binders or that collection of material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It involved matching up the handwritten copies with the electronic printouts, comparing those, ensuring that we had translations for each of those. In some cases ensuring that we had two translations, one for the notebook, handwritten copy and one for the electronic copy, because there were some differences that -- that were notable. It also involved compiling, creating an index and ensuring that the dates and times and participants and user names and summaries were -- were included on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you personally oversee the organisation and essentially the creation of that binder, binder of three -- three-set binder, I should say?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in reviewing the translations that were involved in compiling the material, did you have occasion to make any changes to the translations that you had originally received or originally reviewed?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were occasions where we needed to send them back for revision and sometimes that was because we had been working off of the old printouts where, as we discussed previously, lines were missing at the bottom or lines were missing at the top. Sometimes if the two -- the two versions of the notebook and the electronic copy differed slightly, but we had sometimes two different -- two different translations for each of those documents. So sometimes we asked that they be conformed to essentially one translation but with the notable differences reflected in each of the copies. If that made sense. It was in order to -- to -- to make sure that the translations, as much as possible, reflected the original documents that -- that we were working with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you directly involved in that process?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you rely also in that process on the assistance of other people?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And without telling us who those people were, could you tell us what they did?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were translators, and language assistants mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just move to another area, if I could. Before I get there, could I just ask you if you can recall off the top of your head any specific examples of the types of translation errors that you encountered?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes we asked that a translation be redone even if a word was wrong. One comes to mind where there was a word "narediti" which means to order, and in the translation it came back as "to offer." We thought that was substantial enough, that it was worth having it translated again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In particular with respect to that intercept, was that requested and was that done?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there were also other occasions where we were working -- we had originally worked off of printouts that had been used as analytical documents by the people who -- by the -- by the police in particular, where they underlined certain phrases or sentences in those. So we tried to have, as much as possible, that underlining taken off so that the documents would be as clean as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say that this -- there were analytical documents by the people who -- well, there is an indication here in the transcript, I'm sorry, was a reference to the police in particular. Is that -- is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So you are talking about -- you're talking about intercepts involving the police, the military police?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. Let me clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the first printouts that we received from the police in Tuzla were their working documents, where they had underlined certain sections in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we sent them for translation, they came back with the underlining in them. When we then received the electronic copies, the electronic versions of those identical documents, the clean -- what I'm referring to as clean copies are the ones that we have included in the three-binder set. Therefore, we wanted the translations also to be what I'm calling clean copies, without the underlining in them and without any remarks that would have been placed there by people who were analysing them, the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In other words, to conform with the original document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can I ask -- let me just take to this other area. With respect to the collection of the intercepts, are you aware of whether there remain operators for which -- well, which that -- which have not been identified?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know approximately how many operators with respect to the intercepts that are used -- being used in this case, how many intercepts, I should say, for which an operator hasn't been identified?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall the date?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 28th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to that particular day, are you aware of whether or not there is a notebook entry corresponding to it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is the particular intercept, was that found in the notebooks that were received by the office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And have you personally seen the notebook entry to which that intercept corresponds or that date corresponds?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in your having looked at it, did it appear to you that it had been manipulated or tampered with in any way?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you aware of whether or not the binder collection includes any intercepts of known operators whom -- who have not been called as witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know how many such operators have not been called?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to look at the intercepts that are associated with those two operators?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did those intercepts originate from the notebooks that were furnished to the Prosecution -- to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Are there any intercepts concerning those two operators that are extraneous to the materials that were received by the Office of the Prosecutor from the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "extraneous"?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: They came from some place other than the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And have you personally seen the notebook entries regarding those two operators?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do those entries appear to have been manipulated or tampered with in any way?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And to the best of your recollection, are those entries actually included within the binder collection, or the collection of intercepts used in this case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you develop other material in relation to the binder set, such as indices, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I believe you have indicated that you -- you did that, right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I would just like to briefly -- can I get that displayed on the ELMO, right? I would like you to go through briefly, so that we can -- for the Court's benefit, explain to the Court what those -- what those things are. I think the first thing I'd like to start with are the maps. And I believe -- I would like to have 65 ter 1086 through 1089, please, displayed on e-court. Okay. And I understand we can do it sequentially. Okay. Do you see what's displayed on e-court just now?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just tell us very briefly what these -- what this map is intended to depict?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What's it for?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the top right corner it has the dates of 12 to 13 of July. It was used in a previous case. What it does is it serves as a guide when reading through the intercepts and even the index to the intercepts, because there are so many places that are -- that are discussed in the intercepts. So it's -- it's intended to help orient a person as they're reading through the intercepts. So they -- they can -- so that they can imagine what's happening on the ground and see the proximity of locations. What it also does is really show the sequence. It shows the sequence of the column going through the woods. It shows the sequence of detention and -- and detention locations. And the sequence of events over a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we just take a look at the next one? 1087. And I think that will be it. Okay. Do you see what's in e-court now?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that essentially the same thing and -- the same map and is it for the same purpose?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it's a different map used for the same purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dates on it are the 14th and the 15th of July and so it depicts more the events that were happening on those days, again as reflected in the intercepts and is intended as a guide.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the same for the other two maps that are included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Of course I could do this in cross, but maybe the witness could -- my colleague could ask the witness how she can draw sequence of events from the map. I see a date, I see a time-frame, but I don't see how she can get a sequence of events. Maybe she can explain that. We'll save some time in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to address that with the witness or do you want -- do you prefer to leave it to Mr. Bourgon for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I can address it, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, please. I thank you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think you've heard the question of my esteemed colleague. I guess my question to you is -- first of all, did you draw the map?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is it -- is your understanding of what the map depicts based on information that was furnished to you by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And is that the case with the other maps that are featured as part of the material that accompanied the collection of intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, may I have P02443, please, displayed in e-court. Okay. Do you see what's displayed in e-court now?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's a document entitled, "VRS code-names."

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court briefly what the purpose of this information is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's also intended to help orient anyone reading the intercepts to what the code-names refer to so that they can put the code-names in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is this also essentially something that's put together in order to assist the reader of the collection of material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And are these names that you happened upon yourself or are these names that were provided to you by other people?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are names that were provided -- they were provided by other people. This -- this list was -- was also used in previous cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And these are names that appear in the intercept material itself?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have P02444, please, displayed in e-court. Okay. Do you see what's displayed in e-court now?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It says, "Index of Names, Intercepted Communication" right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Was this list of names developed in order to assist the reader of the material of the intercept material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to these particular names, are these names that you happened upon yourself or are these names and titles information that you derived or was furnished to you by other sources?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: From other people within the Office of the Prosecutor and again it was something that -- it was a list that accompanied the intercepts in previous -- previous trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to the names that are indicated on this list, do those also include the names of some of the accused that are on trial?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to the names of the accused that are on trial, did you notice anything unusual?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell us what, if anything, you noticed?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Mr. Borovcanin's first name is incorrect. It's indicated here as Ljubisa. It should be Ljubomir. And that for General Miletic's name also it's recorded on this document as being Radovan, and it should be Radivoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we just look at the -- there's a second page, at the second page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are four pages to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you scroll down, please. Okay. Thank you very much. You see the second name from the bottom?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And other than that, did any other errors come to your attention or do you recall having seen any other errors with respect to the list of names?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would only say that it's not an exhaustive list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to ask you about, finally, the index that you created, and I'm going to, with the Court's permission, have the witness shown a copy of the binder in which the index is actually contained. And I would like to have her put it on the ELMO, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. What's wrong? Do we have a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could just go through and you could discuss what kind of information is in it if that's all right with the Court and then to the extent that maybe we can get the problem solved in the interim, we might have an opportunity to have a look at it. But I think all of this material had been provided in advance in any event, so hopefully the testimony will just put this in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to be in a position to follow, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know what time the break would be normally scheduled, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The break, I had planned it for 5.23.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We're a little early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But of course if it is more convenient to have the break now to give time, a possibility to the technicians to sort it out, we can have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That would be great. I also have, I believe, the material that I wanted to furnish to Defence counsel as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there is agreement here to have the break now. So shall we restrict it to 20 minutes? 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we are in the process of trying to show the witness the binder. If we could give that a try now, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the ELMO I suppose is back in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, it's on. I can say that. I'm don't know whether it actually works yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Frease, I don't know if it appears this way to the Court, but it appears to be out of focus on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are used to it, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, can you see what's displayed on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit fuzzy but I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Could you just take us from the left-hand column to the right-hand column and tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The left-hand column contains the 65 ter numbers of the individual intercepts. The next column is the date that the intercept was recorded. The next column is the time that it was recorded. The fourth column contains the names of the users, if they're known, the participants, the people who were speaking in the conversation. The fifth column contains the names of other individuals mentioned within the conversation, and the last column on the right is a summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to the users that are indicated in this index, are these the names as they were indicated in the intercepts or are these sort of interpretations of the names that were mentioned in the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these were the names mentioned in the intercepts and all of the information contained here really comes from the intercepts.
